cases.answer: The two papers use human observations differently. Parameswaran et al. (2023) report a molecular association in C9ORF72 FTD/ALS postmortem tissue. Phosphorylated PKR is increased in frontal cortex (especially large pyramidal neurons) of patients carrying C9ORF72 repeat expansions compared with age-matched non-disease controls, and phosphorylated eIF2α (normalised to total eIF2α) is also significantly increased. They conclude this suggests the PKR/eIF2α pathway is activated in C9FTD/ALS patients. It is an association in patients already classed as C9FTD/ALS, not a diagnostic test. Patient-derived iPSC motor neurons (38 days old) showed no difference in p-PKR or p-eIF2α, which the authors interpret as possible later-stage activation. LeBlanc et al. is a single-patient case report in which diagnosis was made by genetic testing. A GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72 was identified and 'confirmed a diagnosis of FTD-ALS'. Post-mortem autopsy then confirmed FTLD with TDP pathology (type C). The clinical workup and SPECT did not give the diagnosis. LeBlanc does not measure PKR or other molecular markers, and Parameswaran does not use PKR phosphorylation for diagnosis.

cases.answer: No. In this PNAS 2024 study (the first author is spelled Sachdeva in the article text, not Sachdev), excising exon 1A (1Ax) silenced sense transcription and eliminated poly-GA, but some poly-GP remained, which must arise from antisense transcript; at least one-third to one-half of poly-GP derives from antisense transcription. Removing the repeat expansion (REx) or the mutant allele eliminated all poly-GP. For network bursting at 3 weeks, C9-unedited and 1Ax motor neurons showed no network bursts, whereas REx and HET(Mut)x neurons did. So exon 1A deletion reproduced repeat-excision effects on neither poly-GP elimination nor network bursting.

remained after excision of exon 1A (Fig. 3C, 1Ax).

cases.ambiguity: Poly-GA was eliminated by 1Ax, so if 'poly-GP elimination' were misread as DPRs generally, it would be partial; for poly-GP specifically the answer is no.

cases.answer: The SPECT result did not agree with the genetic and pathology findings. SPECT showed moderately decreased perfusion in both parietal lobes (left greater than right) with some involvement of the posterior left frontal lobe. The radiologist judged the pattern most in keeping with Alzheimer's disease and not representative of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD). Genetic testing then found a GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9orf72, confirming FTD-ALS. Post-mortem autopsy confirmed FTLD with TDP pathology (international harmonized classification type C). So SPECT interpretation was contradicted by both.

cases.answer: Parameswaran et al. suggest the difference may reflect the model organism. PKR is constitutively and ubiquitously expressed in vertebrate cells, including zebrafish, but is not found in plants, fungi, protists or invertebrates such as Drosophila. They say this may partially explain the differing toxicities of antisense C4G2 repeat RNAs in Drosophila, zebrafish and primary neurons. Drosophila expressing interrupted antisense repeats showed no deficits, whereas the same antisense interrupted (C4G2)108RO construct caused motor axonopathy in zebrafish and was toxic to primary cortical neurons. Experiments supporting the PKR interpretation: (1) PKR reduction partially rescued (C4G2)108RO toxicity in primary cortical neurons (PKR siRNA, Kaplan–Meier cell-death analysis); (2) in zebrafish, co-injecting antisense (C4G2)70 RNA with an eif2ak2 (PKR ortholog) splice-blocking morpholino significantly mitigated axonal length and branching abnormalities, as did a translation-blocking morpholino, whereas the morpholino gave no protection against sense (G4C2)70 RNA.
